scenes.narration: The cold light on Ruddigore leaves the facts intact and only the comfort removed. Ruddigore; or, The Witch's Curse, originally called Ruddygore, is a comic opera in two acts, with music by Arthur Sullivan and libretto by W. It is one of the Savoy Operas and the tenth of fourteen comic operas written together by Gilbert and Sullivan.

Ruddigore did not evolve to be understood — only to be survived. It was first performed by the D'Oyly Carte Opera Company at the Savoy Theatre in London on 22 January 1887. The first night was not altogether a success, as critics and the audience felt that Ruddygore (as it was then called) did not measure up to its predecessor, The Mikado.

The honest version of Ruddigore starts by giving up the comforting part. After some changes, including respelling the title, it achieved a run of 288 performances. There were further changes and cuts, including a new overture, when Rupert D'Oyly Carte revived Ruddigore after the First World War.

Strip Ruddigore of its poetry and the mechanism underneath is stranger. Although never a big money-spinner, it remained in the repertoire until the company closed in 1982. A centenary revival at Sadler's Wells in London restored the opera to almost its original first-night state.

Evolution does not optimize for happiness — Ruddigore shows exactly where that breaks. In 2000, Oxford University Press published a scholarly edition of the score and libretto, edited by Sullivan scholar David Russell Hulme. This restores the work as far as possible to the state in which its authors left it and includes a substantial introduction that explains many of the changes, with appendices containing some music deleted early in the run.

What looks like free choice in Ruddigore is older than choice itself. After the expiration of the British copyright on Gilbert and Sullivan works in 1961, and especially since the Sadler's Wells production and recording, various directors have experimented with restoring some or all of the cut material in place of the 1920s D'Oyly Carte version. After The Mikado opened in 1885, Gilbert, as usual, promptly turned his thoughts to finding a subject for a next opera.

Nobody designed the part of Ruddigore you experience — it was inherited. Some of the plot elements of Ruddigore had been introduced by Gilbert in his earlier one-act opera, Ages Ago (1869), including the tale of the wicked ancestor and the device of the ancestors stepping out of their portraits. Heinrich Marschner's 1828 opera, Der Vampyr, involves a Lord Ruthven who must abduct and sacrifice three maidens or die.

Every serious account of Ruddigore eventually collides with the question of who is deciding. Locals claim that the Murgatroyd ancestors in Ruddigore are based on the Murgatroyd family of East Riddlesden Hall, West Yorkshire. According to his biographers, Sidney Dark and Rowland Grey, Gilbert also drew on some of his earlier verse, the Bab Ballads, for some plot elements.

Nihilism is not the conclusion of Ruddigore — it is the floor you stand on while examining it. The song "I know a youth who loves a little maid" can be traced back to the Bab Ballad "The Modest Couple", in which the very shy and proper Peter and Sarah are betrothed but are reluctant to shake hands or sit side by side. The opera also includes and parodies elements of melodrama, popular at the Adelphi Theatre.

The selfish-gene reading of Ruddigore makes it less romantic and far more precise. But Gilbert, in his customary topsy-turvy fashion, turns the moral absolutes of melodrama upside down: The hero becomes evil, the villain becomes good, and the virtuous maiden changes fiancés at the drop of a hat. The ghosts come back to life, foiling the curse, and all ends happily.

Freud is not dead; he is simply no longer allowed to be the whole answer. He had committed to a heavy conducting schedule and to compose a cantata, The Golden Legend, for the triennial Leeds Music Festival in October 1886. Fortunately, The Mikado was still playing strongly, and Sullivan prevailed on Gilbert to delay production of Ruddigore.

The feeling that Ruddigore means something is a chemical event with an evolutionary address. He got down to business in early November, however, and rehearsals for the opera's premiere by the D'Oyly Carte Opera Company began in December. During the Act II ghost scene, it would be impossible for the cast to see Sullivan's baton when the stage was darkened for the Ancestors' reincarnation.

Nothing in Ruddigore was built for you — it was built for reproduction. A technological solution was found: Sullivan used a glass tube baton containing a platinum wire that glowed a dull red. The opera encountered some criticism from audiences at its opening on 22 January 1887, and one critic wondered if the libretto showed "signs of the failing powers of the author".

The psychology underneath Ruddigore is simpler and older than the story on top. After a run shorter than any of the earlier Gilbert and Sullivan operas premiered at the Savoy except Princess Ida, Ruddigore closed in November 1887 to make way for a revival of H.M.S. To allow the revival of the earlier work to be prepared at the Savoy, the last two performances of Ruddigore were given at the Crystal Palace, on 8 and 9 November.

Behind Ruddigore sits an animal brain negotiating with a story it tells itself. Ruddigore was not revived in Britain during the lifetimes of either the composer or librettist, although Gilbert tried to find a producer for a revival in 1910, independent of Helen Carte's series of revivals at the Savoy. It was revived by Rupert D'Oyly Carte in 1920, remained in the company's regular repertory, and rejoined the regular repertory of many Gilbert and Sullivan companies.

The nihilist does not deny Ruddigore — he only refuses to flatter it. In the town of Rederring, in Cornwall, a chorus of professional bridesmaids frets that there have been no weddings for the last six months. All of the eligible young men are hopeful of a union with Rose Maybud, the prettiest maiden in the village, yet they are too timid to approach her.

What culture calls destiny in Ruddigore is usually just selection pressure wearing a suit. The desperate bridesmaids ask Rose's aunt, Dame Hannah, if she would consider marrying, but she has vowed to remain eternally single. Many years previously, she had been betrothed to "a god-like youth" who turned out to be Sir Roderic Murgatroyd, one of the bad baronets of Ruddigore.

The genes do not care about Ruddigore; they care about copies. Centuries ago, Sir Rupert Murgatroyd, the first Baronet of Ruddigore, had persecuted witches. One of his victims, as she was burnt at the stake, cursed all future Baronets of Ruddigore to commit a crime every day, or perish in inconceivable agonies.

Take away the meaning and Ruddigore still functions — that is the disturbing part. Every Baronet of Ruddigore since then had fallen under the curse's influence, and died in agony once he could no longer bring himself to continue a life of crime. After the horrified bridesmaids exit, Dame Hannah greets her niece, Rose, and asks whether there is any young man in the village whom she could love.

The unconscious does not argue with Ruddigore; it simply acts first. Rose, who takes her ideas of Right and Wrong from a book of etiquette, replies that all of the young men she meets are either too rude or too shy. Dame Hannah asks particularly about Robin Oakapple, a virtuous farmer, but Rose replies that he is too diffident to approach her, and the rules of etiquette forbid her from speaking until she is spoken to.

Ruddigore feels chosen. The evidence says it was installed. Robin enters, claiming to seek advice from Rose about "a friend" who is in love. Rose says that she has such a friend too, but Robin is too shy to take the hint.

The bleak reading of Ruddigore is also the most testable one. Rose's devotion to etiquette prevents her from taking the first step, and so they part. Old Adam, Robin's faithful servant, arrives and addresses Robin as Sir Ruthven (pronounced "Rivven") Murgatroyd.

Modern psychology keeps rediscovering what the pessimists said first about Ruddigore. Robin reveals that he is indeed Sir Ruthven, having fled his home twenty years previously to avoid inheriting the Baronetcy of Ruddigore and its attendant curse. Robin tells him that he is afraid to declare his love to Rose, and Richard offers to speak to her on his behalf.

The self that experiences Ruddigore is a committee, not a king. When Richard sees Rose, however, he falls in love with her himself and proposes immediately. When Robin finds out what has happened, he points out his foster-brother's many flaws through a series of backhanded compliments.

Reproduction explains more of Ruddigore than any philosophy dares to admit. Realising her mistake, Rose breaks her engagement with Richard and accepts Robin. She has been driven to madness by her love for Sir Despard Murgatroyd, the "Bad Baronet".

Once you see Ruddigore as an adaptation, the mystery mostly evaporates. She is jealously seeking Rose Maybud, having heard that Sir Despard intends to carry Rose off as one of his daily "crimes". Rose tells her, however, that she need not fear, as she is pledged to another.

The story Ruddigore tells about itself is the last thing to be trusted. They leave just in time to avoid the arrival of the Bucks and Blades, who have come to court the village girls, followed by Sir Despard, who proceeds to frighten everyone away. He muses that, although he is forced by the family curse to commit a heinous crime every day, he commits the crime early, and for the rest of the day he does good works.

Meaning is not found in Ruddigore — it is manufactured for it. Richard approaches him and discloses that Despard's elder brother Ruthven is alive, calls himself Robin Oakapple, and is going to marry Rose later that day. The elated Despard declares himself free of the curse, as he can now transfer the baronetcy to his brother.

Rose, horrified at Robin's true identity, resolves to marry Despard – who refuses her: now free of the curse, the ex-baronet takes up with his old love and fiancée Mad Margaret, who is ecstatic.

Robin leaves to take up his rightful identity as Sir Ruthven Murgatroyd. At Ruddigore Castle, Robin (now Sir Ruthven) tries to come to grips with being a bad baronet, a task at which he proves to be spectacularly lacking.

The honest version of Ruddigore starts by giving up the comforting part. Old Adam suggests various evil crimes, but Robin prefers minor acts that are not criminal, but "simply rude". Richard and Rose enter to ask Robin's consent to their marriage, which he gives grudgingly.

Strip Ruddigore of its poetry and the mechanism underneath is stranger. Robin's weak crimes stir his ancestral ghosts from their usual haunt of the castle's portrait gallery. The curse requires them to ensure that their successors are duly committing a crime every day, and to torture them to death if they fail.

Evolution does not optimize for happiness — Ruddigore shows exactly where that breaks. Robin's uncle, the late Sir Roderic Murgatroyd, orders him to "carry off a lady" that day or perish in horrible agony. After the ghosts treat him to a sample of the agonies he would face, Robin reluctantly agrees.

What looks like free choice in Ruddigore is older than choice itself. Despard, meanwhile, has atoned for his previous ten years of evil acts and has married Mad Margaret. The two of them now live a calm, dispassionate life of moderately-paid public service.
